A couple of things always jump to my mind when I hear stories/see posts like this:

  • Increases in diagnostic quality/early detection: The biggest thing that seems to come up when you dig a little is that almost routinely the increases in the quantity of a diagnose are the result of changes in the diagnostic criteria or diagnostic methods being used. One of the factors that set off the autism-in-vaccines scare was the result of changes in the diagnostic criteria for autism. So if all you looked at was the number of cases over time, you'd see this sudden, sharp spike in cases. When it comes to conditions like cancer, the quality of the technology matters a lot too. I just spent three years working for a radiology software company, and even just in that amount of time the quality of scanning systems improved noticeably. Not to mention the techniques used to handle the scans. Tumors that would have been missed just five or ten years ago can not only be picked out, but they can be picked out much earlier. So while you may, in fact, be seeing more diagnoses of cancer, that does not necessarily mean there are more instances of cancer - just that we're catching more of them.

  • Age/grouping: As you say, you're getting older. Cancer is going to come up more in older population segments. You didn't mention the details, but there may be environmental or genetic factors in play too. Were any of these people related? Were they smokers? Did they live/work/etc in areas or with materials that might influence their risks? Again, there may be more increases of cancer in your sample set, but is your sample set a (statistically/scientifically) valid set? Also, as you say, as you live longer, you're more likely to meet more people and thus, more likely to encounter more people that have been hit by cancer.

  • Anecdotal/self-bias'ing: We all do this, it's a skill our species developed ages ago and has been important to developing our technologies. We look for patterns, and sometimes we find them where there are none (or there's only the appearance of one). If I counted right, you mentioned seven people. How many people do you know? How many are in your area?

  • Treatment/repeat customers/on-going-fighters: Another factor that you touch on is people that are in an on-going fight. One of the things some of the oncologists I used to work with liked to remind folks of was that you're never really completely cancer free. You're just holding it in check. The long-term survivability stats for cancer patients has gone up a lot in the last twenty years. So it's more (statistically) likely that someone will still be fighting it ten years on because they're still alive to fight it. Likewise, those that have fought and "won" are living long enough (now) that they can have to deal with second and third rounds. And I don't think anyone needs to tell you how hard it is on the body to survive one round, let alone multiple.

Now, that's not to say that there isn't a problem, or to diminish what you/your friends have gone through. That does certainly sound like a lot of cancer for one friend to have to see - especially in young people (that's the part of your post that really did worry me). The key, for me, is that before we say something like "has there been an increase in..." that we're basing it on the clean, quality data.

For what it's worth, I did some quick digging into the stats (http://www.cancer.org/research/cancerfactsstatistics/cancerfactsfigures2015/index) . Death rates - in general - from cancer have been on the decline. I couldn't find/they didn't publish anything about the trends in diagnoses though, which is unfortunate since that was your question. They did list probabilities of developing cancer at given age bands (http://www.cancer.org/acs/groups/content/@editorial/documents/document/acspc-044519.pdf). And, frankly, those are pretty terrifying odds. For males, across all types of invasive cancer, over the course of their lifetime: 43%. Almost half the population. Females only did slightly better (over lifetime) at 38%.

I think it's the combination of food and technology. Lifestyles have changed, and everyone is glued to their computers and/or cell phones more generally. On the other hand, it seems like more people are trying to take measures to prevent cancers.

And, you might be at that age. If you're in your 30s, it'll just go up from here, is my guess. You may be in a place now where you notice more, though.

Tales of Phantasia for the SNES. Amazing combat, great story. Starts small, with your town burning down, slowly find out you're destined to save the world. Mix of strategy and real-time combat.

Exit Fate is a free indie game made to play exactly like Suikoden 2. Probably is a bit longer than Suikoden 2, and has an amazing level scaling system that allows you to level up newcomers in just a couple fights. If you want to avoid emulation, check this game out. Could easily been made into a steam game for $5-$10.

Final Fantasies 4 and 6 probably have the best storylines of any FF games. 4 is probably larger scale, involving the destruction of entire countries. 6 is small scale, largely revolving around a party that's just trying to survive.

Not a JRPG, but a great game nonetheless is E.V.O. for the SNES. Plays a lot like a 2d RPG spore game. Evolve through the ages and become the supreme being.

Mario and Luigi Superstar Saga (and Super Mario RPG) kinda remind me of Earthbound. Not much for story, but great gameplay.

Secret of Evermore is basically Secret of Mana, but instead of a kid in a fantasy world becoming the hero, it's a kid from our world who gets warped, with his dog, through time and tries to fix the time-space continuum. More puzzle based than SoM, but combat is probably harder.

Parasite Eve (PS1) is a tactics RPG. Imagine Resident Evil as a turn based RPG game. You fight corrupted animal-monster things as the only known human that's immune to the effects of this super plague. You use the plague for your own powers as you try and take out the source of it all. Genuinely terrifying game, despite the fact that it's all turn based and 20 years old. I can't imagine what playing this game would have felt like when it came out. Many modern games struggle to do what this game does with shitty graphics.
Ogre Battle 64 is my favorite game of all time. If you like that type of gameplay definitely give it a go. I'd call the story of the game's setting relatable to many modern day countries.
